'''1†.''' To press; constrain; oppress; afflict.
{{smaller block|<poem>And wharfore murned in I go,

{{RunningHeader|twine-holder|6554|twinleaf}}of metal or wire, for holding a ball of twine in a convenient position for unwinding. '''twine-machine''' (twīn′ma̤-shēn″), ''n.'' A spinning-machine for making small cord or string. It is a form of the thread-machine. ''E. H. Knight.'' '''twiner''' (twī′nėr), ''n.'' [< ''twine''1 + ''-er''1.] One who or that which twines. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A machine for twining threads or fibers, as in cotton-spinning.}} {{smaller block|Mules and ''Twiners'' for Spinning Cotton, etc. {{right|''The Engineer'', LXVI. 231.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') A plant which supports itself by twining.}} {{smaller block|Some plants twine with the sun and some twine against it; and most ''twiners'' have nearly allied species that do not climb at all. ''Princeton Rev.'', March, 1878, p. 288.}} '''twine-reeler''' (twīn′rē″lėr), ''n.'' A kind of mule or spinning-machine for making twine or twisting string; a mule-doubler. '''twin-flower''' (twin′flou″ėr), ''n.'' In ''bot.'', a slender creeping and trailing evergreen, ''Linnæa borealis'', with rounded leaves and thread-like branches leafy below, forking near the summit, and bearing a pair of nodding fragrant flowers. {{smaller|The corolla is funnelform, purplish rose-colored or whitish, under half an inch long. The plant is found in cool woods and bogs northward in both hemispheres, in America extending south to the mountains of Maryland and of Colorado and to the Sierra Nevada, from these points reaching within the arctic circle. This modest but extremely beautiful plant was a favorite of Linnæus, who first pointed out its characters and to whom it was dedicated.}} {{smaller block|Beds of purple ''twin-flower.'' {{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 14.}}}} [[File:century v08 p0358 c1f1.png|center|168px]] {{c|{{smaller|Flowering Plant of Twin-flower (''Linnæa borealis'').}}}} '''twinge''' (twinj), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twinged'', ppr. ''twinging''. [(''a'') < ME. ''twingen'', appar. altered from *''thwingen'', < AS. *''thwingan'' (pret. *''thwang'') = OS. ''thwingan'' = OFries. ''dwinga'', ''twinga'' = MD. ''dwinghen'', D. ''dwingen'' = OHG. ''dwingan'', ''thwingan'', press, constrain, oppress, conquer, MHG. ''twingen'', ''dwingen'', G. ''zwingen'' = Icel. ''thvinga'', weigh down, oppress, compel, = Dan. ''tvinge'' = Sw. ''tvinga'', constrain. (''b'') < ME. ''twengen'' = MD. ''dwenghen'' = OHG. ''zwengan'', ''dwengan'', MHG. ''twengen'', G. ''zwangen'', press, constrain, a secondary verb (associated with the noun, OHG. ''zwang'', ''dwang'', ''gidwang'', MHG. ''zwanc'', ''twanc'', G. ''zwang'', constraint, compulsion), from the orig. strong verb above. Cf. ''thong'', from the same ult. source.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To press; constrain; oppress; afflict. {{smaller block|And wharfore murned in I go, Whil that ''twinges'' me the fo? {{right|''Anglo-Saxon and Early Eng. Psalter'' (ed. Stevenson, 1843), [xli. 10.}}}} '''2.''' To pull with a sharp, pinching jerk; tweak; twitch. {{smaller block|He ''twengde'' & schok hire [the Devil] bi the nose that the fur [fire] out-blaste. {{right|''Rob. of Gloucester'', St. Dunstan, l. 81. (''Morris and Skeat'', [II. 22.)}} ''Twinge'' three or four buttons From off my lady’s gown. {{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, i. 1.}} When a man is past his sense, There ’s no way to reduce him thence But ''twinging'' him by th’ ears and nose, Or laying on of heavy blows. {{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, III. i. 1155.}}}} '''3.''' To torment with sharp, darting pains; sting: said of physical or mental pain. {{smaller block|The gnat charged into the nostrils of the lion, and there ''twinged'' him till he made him tear himself, and so mastered him. {{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}} {{smaller block|The poor wretch has a little shrivelled bit of conscience left. It ''twinges'' him sometimes, like a dying nerve in a rotten tooth. {{right|''T. Winthrop'', Cecil Dreeme, v.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To have a sharp, jerking pain, like a twitch; suffer a keen, shooting pain. {{smaller block|I’ve a ''twinging'' knee Oft hinders dancing. {{right|''George Eliot'', Spanish Gypsy, i.}}}} '''twinge''' (twinj), ''n.'' [< ''twinge'', ''v.''] '''1.''' A nipping or pinching; a twitch; a tweak. {{smaller block|blows and ''twinges'' by the ears.{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}} '''2.''' A sharp, darting pain of momentary continuance; a pang, physical or mental. {{smaller block|The wickedness of this old villain startles me, and gives me a ''twinge'' for my own sin, tho’ it come far short of his.{{right|''Dryden'', Spanish Friar, iv. 1.}} “What is it, my dear child?” cries kind Mrs. Lambert, as he started. “Nothing, Madam; a ''twinge'' in my shoulder,” said the lad.{{right|''Thackeray'', Virginians, xxii.}}}} ='''Syn. 2.''' See ''pain''1 and ''agony''. '''twingle-twangle†''' (twing′gl-twang″gl), ''n.'' [A varied redupl. of ''twangle''.] A twangling sound; a jangle. {{smaller block|With the rare discord of bells, pipes, and tabors, Hotch-potch of Scotch and Irish ''twingle-twangles.''{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, iii. 2.}}}} '''twining''' (twī′ning), ''p. a.'' Twisting; winding; coiling; embracing. —'''Twining stem''', {{smaller|in ''bot.'', a stem which ascends spirally around another stem, a branch, or a prop, either to the right or to the left. See ''right-handed'', 3.}} '''twiningly''' (twī′ning-li), ''adv.'' In a twining manner; by twining. ''Bailey'', 1731. '''twink'''1 (twingk), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''twinken'', ''twynken'', < AS. *''twincan'' (=MHG. ''zwinken'', ''zwingen''), wink. {{img float|file=century v08 p0358 c2f1.png|width=109px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Twining Stems.
1, Hedge-bindweed, ''Convolvulus'' (''Calystegia'') ''sepium''; 2, Hop, ''Humulus Lupulus''.}}}} Hence ''twinkle.''] To wink. [Obsolete or prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|''Twynkyn,'' with the eye. . . . Conquinisco. {{right|''Prompt. Parv.,'' p. 505.}}}} {{smaller block|Some turne the whites up, some looke to the foote, Some winke, some ''twinke,'' some blinke, some stare as fast. {{right|''Lane,'' Tom Tel-Troths Message (1600). (''Nares.'')}}}} ¶'''twink'''1 (twingk), ''n.'' [< ''twink''1, ''v.''] A wink; a twinkling. {{smaller block|But in a ''twinck'' methought ’A chang’d at once his habit and his steed. {{right|''Peele,'' Honour of the Garter.}}}} '''twink'''2 (twingk), ''v. t.'' [Imitative; cf. ''tink''1 and ''twank.''] To pour out in bird-notes; twitter; chirp. {{smaller block|As a swallow in the air doth sing With no continued tune, but, pausing still, ''Twinks'' out her scatter’d voice in accents shrill. {{right|''Chapman,'' Odyssey, xxi. 548.}}}} '''twink'''2 (twingk), ''n.'' [Cf. ''twink''2, ''v.,'' also ''pink, spink, finch,'' etc.] The chaffinch. '''twinkle''' (twing′kl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twinkled,'' ppr. ''twinkling.'' [Early mod. E. ''twynkle, twynkell;'' < ME. ''twinclen, twynclen,'' < AS. ''twinclian,'' twinkle; freq. of *''twincan,'' wink: see ''twink''1.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To shut an eye or the eyes with an involuntary twitch or with a quick voluntary and significant action; blink; wink. {{smaller block|She hath now ''twyncled'' fyrst upon the with wyckede eye. {{right|''Chaucer,'' Boëthius, ii. prose 3.}}}} {{smaller block|I ''twynkell'' with the eye. Je clignette. . . . You ''twynkell'' with your eye, do you? I truste you never the better. {{right|''Palsgrave,'' p. 764.}}}} {{smaller block|The owl fell a moping and ''twinkling.'' {{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}} '''2.''' Of the eyelids, to open and shut with frequent involuntary twitches; hence, of anything that moves rapidly, to dart to and fro. {{smaller block|Myne eye ''twynkleth'' somtyme and I can nat cease it. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 764.}} No lips so sweet That I may worship them? No eyelids meet To ''twinkle'' on my bosom? {{right|''Keats'', Endymion, iv.}} The feet of said partner never ceased to ''twinkle'' in and out from beneath her skirts. {{right|''New York Evening Post'', April 25, 1891.}}}} '''3.''' To pass in and out of sight rapidly, as a light; flash at almost insensible intervals; shine with quick, irregular gleams; scintillate; sparkle, as a star. {{smaller block|All the fixed Tapers He made to ''twinkle'' with such trembling capers. {{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 4.}} The chiefe Mountaines, them of Pennobscot, the ''twinkling'' Mountaine of Acocisco, the great Mountaine of Sassanow, and the high Mountaine of Massachuset. {{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 195.}} Here plots of sparkling water tremble bright With thousand thousand ''twinkling'' points of light. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Evening Walk.}} I see his gray eyes ''twinkle'' yet At his own jest. {{right|''Tennyson'', Miller’s Daughter.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To open and shut rapidly; wink; blink. {{smaller block|drop.{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xiv.}}}} {{smaller block|The bats whirled . . . their wings and ''twinkled'' their small eyes.{{right|''Disraeli'', Alroy, x. 17.}}}} '''2.''' To emit in quick gleams; flash out. {{smaller block|The sun and moon also Thou mad’st to give him light; And each one of the wandring stars to ''twinkle'' sparkles bright.{{right|''Surrey'', Paraphrase of Ps. viii.}}}} '''3.''' To influence or charm by sparkling. {{smaller block|That affectionate light, those diamond things, Those eyes, those passions, those supreme pearl springs, Shall be my grief, or ''twinkle'' me to pleasure.{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, iv.}}}} '''twinkle''' (twing′kl), ''n.'' [< ''twinkle'', ''v.''] '''1.''' A twitching of the eyelid; a blinking; a wink. {{smaller block|Old David moved from place to place about his ordinary employments, scarce shewing, unless by . . . an occasional convulsive sigh, or ''twinkle'' of the eyelid, that he was labouring under the yoke of such bitter affliction.{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xiv.}}}} '''2.''' A quick, tremulous light; a glimmer; a sparkle; a flash. {{smaller block|Glimmers and dies the fire-fly’s spark — Like starry ''twinkles'' that momently break Through the rifts of the gathering tempest’s rack.{{right|''J. R. Drake'', Culprit Fay.}}}} '''3.''' The time required for a wink; a twinkling. '''twinkler''' (twing′klėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''twynclere'' (= MHG. ''zwinkeler''); < ''twinkle'' + ''-er''1.] One who or that which twinkles. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A winker; a blinker; especially, the eye.}} {{smaller block|The ''twynclere'' with the eȝe forgeth wicke thingus.{{right|''Wyclif'', Ecclus. xxvii. 25.}}}} {{smaller block|You’ll just be pleased . . . not to be staring at me, following me up and down with those ''twinklers'' of yours.{{right|''Marryatt'', Snarleyyow, I. vii.}}}} (''b'') That which glimmers, sparkles, or flashes; a sparkler. {{smaller block|''Aram.'' The stars have done this.
''Clar.'' The pretty little ''twinklers.'' {{right|''Vanbrugh'', Confederacy, iii. 2.}} Such tiny ''twinklers'' as the planet-orbs That there attendant on the solar power With borrowed light pursued their narrower way. {{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, ix.}}}} '''twinkling''' (twing′kling), ''n.'' [< ME. ''twinkling'', ''twinkelinge''; verbal n. of ''twinkle'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of one who or that which twinkles; especially, a quick twitching or fluttering movement of the eye; a wink. {{smaller block|Boys in their first bloom, skilled in the dance, . . . smote the good floor with their feet. And Odysseus gazed at the ''twinklings'' of the feet, and marvelled in spirit. {{right|''Butcher and Lang'', tr. of Homer’s Odyssey, viii. (ed. Macmillan, 1881, p. 123).}}}} '''2.''' The phenomenon of scintillation of the fixed stars, consisting of fluctuations of light and of color at the rate of from fifty to a hundred per second. {{smaller|The fluctuations of light did not escape the notice of the ancients; those of color were noticed by Robert Hooke in 1665. The phenomenon was, without any reason at all, generally supposed to have its origin in the eye, until William Nicholson, the chemist, showed in 1813 that, if the image of a twinkling star was stretched out into a ribbon by an irregular movement of the telescope, the fluctuations would appear as variations of light and color along this ribbon. Charles Dufour, in 1856, published the following generalizations of his observations, now known as ''Dufour’s laws:'' (1) the pale stars twinkle more than the chrome, and the chrome more than the ruddy ones; (2) at different altitudes the twinkling is proportional to the coefficient of astronomical refraction multiplied by the trajectory of the ray; and (3) the twinkling diminishes as the diameter of the star increases. Lorenzo Respighi, in 1868, examined the effect of twinkling upon the spectra of stars. He found that oblique bands of shade pass over the spectrum in different directions according as the star is east or west of the meridian. Finally, Charles Montigny, with a special instrument called a scintillometer, has made extensive observations concerning the differences of the rate of twinkling at different seasons, under different meteorological conditions, and for different stars. It is certain that twinkling is due in some way to the entrance and passage of the light in the atmosphere, but how is not altogether settled. Twinkling is entirely distinct from the “dancing” of stars, which is frequent, especially in winter.}} '''3.''' The time required for one twinkle or wink, as of the eye; a flash; hence, a very short time. {{smaller block|This world in an iȝes ''twynkeling'' Thou maist distroie, noon may defende. {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 173.}} We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the ''twinkling'' of an eye, at the last trump. {{right|1 Cor. xv. 51, 52.}} ''Ric.'' What you do, do in a ''twinkling'', sir. ''Val.'' As soon as may be. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, iv. 2.}} He vanish’d frae her sight, Wi’ the ''twinkling'' o’ an eye. {{right|''Courteous Knight'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 277).}} Or in a ''twinkling'' of this true blue steel. {{right|''Sir H. Taylor'', Philip van Artevelde, II., iii. 1.}}}} '''In the twinkling of a bedpost.''' {{smaller|See ''bedpost''.}} '''twinleaf''' (twin′lēf), ''n.'' An American herb, ''Jeffersonia diphylla'': so named from the pair of leaflets into which the blade of the leaf is divided. See cut on following page.
